title: Explaining Near-Zero Hessian Eigenvalues Through Approximate Symmetries in Neural Networks
abstract: The Hessian of the training loss governs the local geometry of the loss landscape, yet despite existing explanations for its largest eigenvalues, the origin of the vast multitude of vanishingly small eigenvalues remains elusive. We argue that the bulk consists of the weakly lifted pseudo-Goldstone modes of the continuous symmetries of the network parametrization. In deep linear networks these symmetries are exact: they generate flat directions and hence exact zero modes, whose eigenvectors we construct explicitly. Introducing a ReLU nonlinearity as a perturbation, we show that it breaks these symmetries weakly and explicitly. Resolving the spectrum at the level of eigenvectors, we find that the high-curvature directions are orthogonal to the symmetry subspace, while the bulk lies almost entirely within it. We demonstrate the mechanism in a two-layer ReLU student--teacher model and in a network trained on CIFAR-10. A convolutional example demonstrates that the same diagnostic extends beyond fully connected layers. Together, these results link the Hessian bulk to weakly broken symmetries and clarify the origin of near-zero modes.
summary: This work explains that the vast number of near-zero eigenvalues in neural network loss functions are not random artifacts but rather signatures of approximate continuous symmetries inherent in the network's structure. By analyzing how these symmetries are weakly broken by nonlinearities, the authors provide a deep physical understanding of low-curvature directions in ML optimization.
main_problem: The paper addresses the mystery of near-zero eigenvalues in the Hessian matrix of a neural network's loss landscape.
main_result: It argues that this bulk of small eigenvalues originates from pseudo-Goldstone modes associated with continuous symmetries of the network parametrization, which are only weakly broken by nonlinearities like ReLU.
method: The analysis involves studying the Hessian spectrum by constructing an adiabatic path between a perfectly symmetric linear limit and the full nonlinear model using perturbation theory and eigenvector overlap calculations.
model_or_system: The system is deep neural networks, analyzed through their loss function's Hessian matrix. The study progresses from simple two-layer linear models to complex convolutional architectures trained on datasets like CIFAR-10.
key_observables: Hessian eigenvalues spectrum (large outliers vs. small bulk), overlap ($	ext{o}_i$) between eigenvectors and the symmetry subspace, and eigenvalue scaling laws ($\epsilon^2$).
important_parameters: The perturbation strength $\epsilon$ controlling the transition from linear to nonlinear regimes; network depth and architecture (e.g., convolutional layers).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that symmetries are continuous and relies on comparing the Hessian at an endpoint of training rather than an exact critical point.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of eigenvalues as symmetry is broken ($\epsilon^2$ scaling) and show eigenvector overlap measurements comparing periodic vs. nonperiodic boundary conditions in CNNs.
paper_structure: The paper builds its argument by first establishing exact zero modes in linear networks, then perturbing this system with ReLU to generate pseudo-Goldstone modes, and finally generalizing the diagnostic tool (overlap measurement) to complex convolutional architectures.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful analogy linking concepts from condensed matter physics—specifically Goldstone theorems related to broken continuous symmetries—to the geometry of high-dimensional machine learning loss landscapes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Symmetries in fully connected layers. Left: original network, two hidden neurons highlighted. Middle: discrete permutation symmetry, swapping incoming and outgoing con- nections of two hidden units. Holds for any activation. Right: continuous symmetry of linear networks, an infinitesimal ro- tation of the incoming weights compensated on the outgoing weights. Preserves the output and generates a zero mode.

Ranked Hessian eigenvalues of the two-layer Leaky- ReLU student–teacher model (N = 20, C = 3, single draw of Gaussian teacher weights W(k) ij ∼N(0, σ2) with σ2 = 1/N) as a function of the symmetry-breaking strength ε, from the linear network (ε →0) to ReLU (ε = 1). “NC+C” and “NC+C+1” are the modes bordering the gap. The bulk eigenvalues, zero at ε = 0, rise as ε2 and follow the eigen- values of the projected block PH(ε)P (dashed lines). The N rescaling zero modes stay at zero for all ε, below the plotted range. A small group of C modes (orange, the mean-gradient outliers) bends near ε ≈0.5 to merge with the large block. The clean ε2 trend without ε4 bending indicates eigenvectors...

FIG. 3. Two-layer student–teacher model of Fig. 2, Hessian at the global minimum. Top: ReLU (green) and linear (orange) spectra. The linear network has NC = 60 finite eigenvalues, the ReLU network has C = 3 additional large eigenvalues due to nonzero ⟨∂θf ⊤⟩x. Bottom: overlap oi (8) between ReLU eigenvectors and the linear symmetry subspace. Small- eigenvalue modes have oi ≈1, revealing alignment with linear symmetry directions. The leading NC+C modes are strongly suppressed (random baseline orandom ≈0.87).

FIG. 4. Three-layer ReLU network trained on CIFAR-10, with effective dimensions Neff = 100, Ceff = 9. Overlap oi (8) between the largest 5,000 ReLU Hessian eigenvectors and the symmetry subspace P of the linear comparison model. Apart from Ceff = 9 leading outliers, only modes beyond the NeffCeff = 900 largest reach oi ≈1. The random base- line is orandom ≈0.998 (standard deviation ≈10−4), so the leading modes are suppressed by hundreds to thousands of standard deviations. The cumulative coverage (9) reaches O5000 ≈0.95, implying the unmeasured tail is almost entirely symmetric.

FIG. 5. Convolutional student–teacher network (10), input width 200, hidden width N = 190, kernel width K = 11, mean-squared error, Hessian at identical student/teacher pa- rameters drawn once from a Gaussian. Overlap between the eigenvectors of the nonperiodic-network Hessian and the K = 11 symmetry directions of the corresponding periodic network, for the 60 smallest eigenvalues. The random base- line is K/d ≈0.055 (dashed). Although the boundary condi- tions break the exact symmetry, the smallest K modes retain near-unity overlap.
